Thus ax+1 and bx+1 have reduced denominators v/d_a and v/d_b; their being rational squares implies v=d_a r^2=d_b s^2 and au+v=d_a A_1^2, bu+v=d_b B_1^2, including the zero-numerator case.","scope":"All stated common neighbors; r,s are positive integers and A_1,B_1 are nonnegative integers."},{"claim":"When e>max(alpha,beta), p divides v but not u, and v_p(d_a)=alpha, v_p(d_b)=beta. Dividing the numerator-square equations by the corresponding powers of p and reducing modulo p yields nonzero congruences a_0u ≡ d_{a,0}A_1^2 and b_0u ≡ d_{b,0}B_1^2; hence A_1 and B_1 are nonzero modulo p.","scope":"The high-denominator hypothesis ensures the discarded terms v/p^alpha and v/p^beta vanish modulo p."},{"claim":"Dividing the two nonzero congruences gives (A_1/B_1)^2 ≡ (a_0/b_0)(d_{b,0}/d_{a,0}) mod p. The denominator-square relation gives d_b/d_a=(r/s)^2 and beta-alpha=2k for k=v_p(r/s), so d_{b,0}/d_{a,0}=((r/s)/p^k)^2 is a p-adic unit square. Therefore a_0/b_0 is a nonzero quadratic residue modulo p.","scope":"The reduction and ratio are valid because all denominators involved are p-units; the contrapositive yields the stated bound when the residue is a nonresidue."}],"citation_checks":[],"external_dependency_coverage":{"complete":true,"undeclared_external_results":[]}}]}}
